mix.name: Healthy mix
mix.desc: A bit of everything, at your level. You don't know the theme in advance, just like in a real game.
spot: Before calculating, scan checks, captures and threats for both sides.
Ask what your opponent's last move changed: what does it attack, and what did it stop defending?
mix.hint: Start with forcing moves: checks, captures, threats.

opening.name: Opening
opening.desc: Tactics in the first phase of the game, often punishing slow development or a king left in the centre.
spot: Kings still in the centre and loose pieces on b7/b2 are common targets.
Look for tricks on f7/f2 and pins on the e-file or the a4–e8 diagonal.
opening.hint: Something in the opponent's setup is loose. Find the forcing move.

middlegame.name: Middlegame
middlegame.desc: Tactics in the second phase of the game, with most pieces still on the board.
spot: Count attackers and defenders on every contested piece.
Pieces defended only once, or only by the king, are the first candidates.
middlegame.hint: Find the weakest enemy piece or square and hit it with tempo.

endgame.name: Endgame
endgame.desc: Tactics in the final phase, where every pawn and tempo counts.
spot: Passed pawns and an active king outweigh small material gains.
A trade that gains a tempo can decide a pawn race.
endgame.hint: Think about the pawns: who promotes first, and can you deflect the defender?

rookEndgame.name: Rook endgame
rookEndgame.desc: Endgames with only rooks and pawns, the most common endgame there is.
spot: Rooks belong behind passed pawns, yours or theirs.
Watch for skewers along ranks and checks that win the rook.
rookEndgame.hint: Activate the rook or king, or look for a skewer along a rank or file.

bishopEndgame.name: Bishop endgame
bishopEndgame.desc: Endgames with only bishops and pawns.
spot: Opposite-coloured bishops are drawish. With same-coloured bishops, which colour the pawns stand on matters.
A bishop can stop a passer from far away, so deflect it.
bishopEndgame.hint: Which pawn can the enemy bishop not control?

pawnEndgame.name: Pawn endgame
pawnEndgame.desc: Only kings and pawns. Every tempo decides the result.
spot: Count tempi: who queens first, and does anyone queen with check?
Opposition, the square of the pawn and breakthroughs decide most of these.
pawnEndgame.hint: Count moves to promotion for both sides before you touch the king.

knightEndgame.name: Knight endgame
knightEndgame.desc: Endgames with only knights and pawns.
spot: Knights struggle against rook pawns and far-apart passers.
A knight fork can win the defending knight or cover the queening square.
knightEndgame.hint: Look for a knight fork, or a pawn the knight can't catch.

queenEndgame.name: Queen endgame
queenEndgame.desc: Endgames with only queens and pawns.
spot: Checks decide everything. Look for a skewer or a check that forces the queen trade.
A passed pawn supported by the queen is a monster.
queenEndgame.hint: Find a check that wins the queen or forces a winning pawn ending.

queenRookEndgame.name: Queen and rook
queenRookEndgame.desc: Endgames with only queens, rooks and pawns.
spot: Back-rank weaknesses and loose rooks are frequent targets.
A queen and rook battery on an open file can mate.
queenRookEndgame.hint: Look at the back rank and any undefended rook.

advancedPawn.name: Advanced pawn
advancedPawn.desc: One of your pawns is deep in enemy territory, often threatening to promote.
spot: A pawn on the seventh rank ties pieces down. Count its blockers.
Deflect or remove the piece that stops it.
advancedPawn.hint: Your far-advanced pawn is the hero. What is stopping it from promoting?

attackingF2F7.name: Attacking f2 or f7
attackingF2F7.desc: An attack on the f2 or f7 pawn, which only the king guards early on. Think Fried Liver.
spot: Before castling, f7/f2 is defended only by the king.
Bishop on c4/c5 plus a knight or queen aiming at f7/f2 is the classic battery.
attackingF2F7.hint: The f7/f2 square is weak. What can land there?

capturingDefender.name: Capture the defender
capturingDefender.desc: Remove the piece guarding something important, then take what it was guarding.
spot: For each enemy piece, ask what defends it. Can you take that defender?
A capture that looks like an even trade often wins a piece a move later.
capturingDefender.hint: One enemy piece has a vital defensive job. Remove it.

discoveredAttack.name: Discovered attack
discoveredAttack.desc: Move one piece out of the way to unmask an attack by the rook, bishop or queen behind it.
spot: Look for your own line pieces blocked by your own pieces.
The piece that moves can make its own threat: two threats at once.
discoveredAttack.hint: One of your long-range pieces is hiding behind another. Move the front one with a threat.

doubleCheck.name: Double check
doubleCheck.desc: Check with two pieces at once. Nothing can block or capture both, so the king must move.
spot: A discovered check where the moving piece also gives check.
With the king forced to move, mate is often close.
doubleCheck.hint: Can you give check with two pieces at once?

exposedKing.name: Exposed king
exposedKing.desc: A king with few defenders around it, usually leading to mate or a big material gain.
spot: A missing pawn shield means open lines for your rooks and queen.
Play the checks that bring new pieces into the attack first.
exposedKing.hint: The enemy king is short of defenders. Start with a forcing check.

fork.name: Fork
fork.desc: One move attacks two or more enemy pieces at once.
spot: Look for a square where one piece would hit two valuable or loose targets.
Knight forks hide well. Check every square your knight can jump to.
Checks make the strongest forks, because the king has to answer first.
fork.hint: Find a square where one piece attacks two targets at once.

hangingPiece.name: Hanging piece
hangingPiece.desc: An enemy piece is undefended or under-defended. It's free to take.
spot: After every opponent move, list what's attacked and what's defended.
Before taking, make sure the capture doesn't walk into a recapture or a mate threat.
hangingPiece.hint: Something is free. Count attackers and defenders on each enemy piece.

kingsideAttack.name: Kingside attack
kingsideAttack.desc: An attack on a king that castled short.
spot: Typical targets are h7/h2, g7/g2 and the f-file.
Sacrifices on h6, g6 or h7 rip the king's cover open.
kingsideAttack.hint: Hit the castled king. The pawn shield is the weak point.

pin.name: Pin
pin.desc: A piece can't move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it.
spot: Look for two enemy pieces on one line, with your bishop, rook or queen able to reach it.
Attack a pinned piece again, because it can't run.
Pinned pieces don't really defend.
pin.hint: Look for enemy pieces lined up with their king or queen.

queensideAttack.name: Queenside attack
queensideAttack.desc: An attack on a king that castled long.
spot: The a- and b-pawns and the c-file are the ways in.
Sacrifices on b7/b2 or a6/a3 open the king up.
queensideAttack.hint: The king on the queenside has thin cover. Open a line.

sacrifice.name: Sacrifice
sacrifice.desc: Give up material now to win more, or mate, after a forced sequence.
spot: Ask what would happen if a key defender disappeared.
Sacrifices work when every reply is forced: checks and captures.
sacrifice.hint: Material matters less than it looks here. Which forcing sacrifice works?

skewer.name: Skewer
skewer.desc: Attack a valuable piece that has to move, exposing the piece behind it. The reverse of a pin.
spot: Look for king and queen, or queen and rook, on one line.
A check along a line often skewers the king to something behind it.
skewer.hint: Two enemy pieces share a line, with the more valuable one in front.

trappedPiece.name: Trapped piece
trappedPiece.desc: An enemy piece has no safe squares and can be won.
spot: Bishops on a7/h7, knights on the rim and queens grabbing b2 get trapped often.
Take away the escape squares first, then attack.
trappedPiece.hint: One enemy piece has nowhere to go. Attack it.

attraction.name: Attraction
attraction.desc: Force an enemy piece onto a square where it becomes a target, usually with a sacrifice.
spot: It often lures the king into a check or a knight fork.
The sacrificed piece is bait. Where do you want their piece to stand?
attraction.hint: Lure an enemy piece onto a fatal square.

clearance.name: Clearance
clearance.desc: Vacate a square, file or diagonal, often with tempo, so another piece can use it.
spot: One of your own pieces is in the way of a winning move.
Move it with a threat so the opponent has no time to react.
clearance.hint: One of your pieces is in the way. Clear it with tempo.

collinearMove.name: Collinear move
collinearMove.desc: Two opposing line pieces face each other, and one slides along that line without capturing.
spot: The line between the two pieces matters more than the capture.
It often keeps a pin alive or sets up a discovery.
collinearMove.hint: Slide along the line instead of capturing.

discoveredCheck.name: Discovered check
discoveredCheck.desc: Move a piece to reveal check from the piece behind it. The moving piece can then grab almost anything.
spot: The moving piece is free to capture, fork or attack the queen.
Repeated discovered checks (a windmill) can strip the whole position.
discoveredCheck.hint: Unmask a check, and use the moving piece to win something.

defensiveMove.name: Defensive move
defensiveMove.desc: Find the one precise move that avoids losing material or the game.
spot: First name every threat your opponent is making.
The best defence often counter-attacks.
defensiveMove.hint: What is your opponent threatening? Find the only move that stops it.

deflection.name: Deflection
deflection.desc: Distract a defender from a key duty. Also called overloading.
spot: Find a defender doing two jobs at once.
Offer it something it has to take, then exploit what it stopped guarding.
deflection.hint: One enemy piece is overloaded. Give it a second job.

interference.name: Interference
interference.desc: Put a piece between an enemy piece and what it defends, cutting the connection.
spot: Look for two enemy pieces defending each other along a line.
A piece on the crossing square can break both duties.
interference.hint: Cut the line between an enemy defender and what it defends.

intermezzo.name: Intermezzo
intermezzo.desc: Before the expected move, insert a forcing move your opponent has to answer. Also called a zwischenzug.
spot: Don't recapture on autopilot. Is there a check or a bigger threat first?
The in-between move usually improves your follow-up.
intermezzo.hint: Don't play the obvious recapture yet. Is there a stronger forcing move first?

quietMove.name: Quiet move
quietMove.desc: No check, capture or direct threat, but it sets up a threat that can't be stopped.
spot: When the forcing moves fail, look for a move that takes away escape squares.
Quiet moves often prepare mate or trap a piece.
quietMove.hint: No check or capture works. Find the calm move that leaves an unstoppable threat.

xRayAttack.name: X-ray attack
xRayAttack.desc: A piece attacks or defends a square through an enemy piece.
spot: After a trade on a line, the piece behind still controls the square.
Count x-ray defenders when deciding whether a capture works.
xRayAttack.hint: Look through an enemy piece along a line.

zugzwang.name: Zugzwang
zugzwang.desc: Every move the opponent has makes their position worse.
spot: Sometimes the strongest move is a waiting move.
Common in pawn endgames: take the opposition and make them move.
zugzwang.hint: Leave the opponent with only bad moves. A waiting move may do it.

mate.name: Checkmate
mate.desc: Win the game with style. Every puzzle here ends in mate.
spot: Checks first, then captures, then threats.
Find the king's escape squares, take them away, then check.
mate.hint: There is a forced mate. Start with checks.

mateIn1.name: Mate in 1
spot: List every check. One of them mates.
Look at the king's escape squares.
mateIn1.hint: One of your checks is mate.

mateIn2.name: Mate in 2
spot: The first move is often a sacrifice, or a quiet move that cuts off squares.
Ask which mate you'd threaten if it were your move again.
mateIn2.hint: Find a move that leaves no defence against mate next move.

mateIn3.name: Mate in 3
spot: Forcing moves keep the tree small, so start with checks.
Picture the final mating net, then work backwards.
mateIn3.hint: Picture the final mating position, then find the checks that force it.

mateIn4.name: Mate in 4
spot: Long mates are usually a chain of checks. Find the one that doesn't let the king out.
Sacrifices that strip the pawn cover are common.
mateIn4.hint: A long chain of checks. Keep the king in the box.

mateIn5.name: Mate in 5 or more
mateIn5.desc: Work out a long mating sequence.
spot: Find the mating pattern you're aiming for first.
Every move should be forcing. If it isn't, the opponent gets a tempo.
mateIn5.hint: Identify the final mating pattern, then force the king there.

backRankMate.name: Back rank mate
backRankMate.desc: Mate on the home rank, with the king trapped behind its own pawns.
spot: No luft (h3/h6) and only one back-rank defender spells danger.
Deflect or overload that defender.
backRankMate.hint: The king is stuck behind its pawns. Who guards the back rank?

smotheredMate.name: Smothered mate
smotheredMate.desc: A knight mates a king completely surrounded by its own pieces.
spot: The classic: a queen check on g8 forces Rxg8, then Nf7#.
The king's own pieces become the cage.
smotheredMate.hint: The king is surrounded by its own pieces. Could a knight check be mate?

anastasiaMate.name: Anastasia's mate
anastasiaMate.desc: A knight and a rook or queen trap the king on the edge, boxed in by one of its own pieces.
spot: The knight (often on e7/e2) covers the escape squares, and the heavy piece mates along the edge file.
anastasiaMate.hint: The knight cuts off the escape squares and a heavy piece mates on the edge file.

arabianMate.name: Arabian mate
arabianMate.desc: A knight and a rook trap the king in a corner.
spot: The rook next to the cornered king, defended by a knight that also covers the escape square.
arabianMate.hint: Put the rook next to the cornered king, protected by a knight.

bodenMate.name: Boden's mate
bodenMate.desc: Two bishops on criss-crossing diagonals mate a king boxed in by its own pieces.
spot: Often after long castling: a sacrifice on c6/c3 opens the diagonal.

doubleBishopMate.name: Double bishop mate
doubleBishopMate.desc: Two bishops on neighbouring diagonals mate a king blocked by its own pieces.
spot: One bishop checks while the other covers the only escape diagonal.
doubleBishopMate.hint: Two bishops side by side on parallel diagonals.

dovetailMate.name: Dovetail mate
dovetailMate.desc: The queen mates a king on the next square, whose two escape squares are blocked by its own pieces.
spot: A defended queen diagonally next to the king, with the king's own pieces blocking its retreat.
dovetailMate.hint: A protected queen right next to the king.

epauletteMate.name: Epaulette mate
epauletteMate.desc: The king's two side squares are blocked by its own pieces, like epaulettes, and a check from the front mates.
spot: Rooks on either side of the king are the classic epaulettes.
A queen check on the king's file, from in front, finishes.
epauletteMate.hint: The king's own pieces block both sides. Check it from the front.

hookMate.name: Hook mate
hookMate.desc: Rook, knight and pawn combine, with an enemy pawn blocking the king's escape.
spot: The knight defends the rook, and your pawn defends the knight.
hookMate.hint: Rook, protected by a knight, protected by a pawn.

killBoxMate.name: Kill box mate
killBoxMate.desc: A rook next to the king, backed by the queen, which also covers the escape squares. The king is caught in a 3×3 box.
spot: The queen protects the rook diagonally and seals the box.
killBoxMate.hint: Rook next to the king, queen behind it on the diagonal.

pillsburysMate.name: Pillsbury's mate
pillsburysMate.desc: A rook mates the king while a bishop helps to confine it.
spot: Often on the g-file against a king on h8, with the bishop on the long diagonal.
pillsburysMate.hint: Rook mates on the file, with the bishop covering the diagonal.

morphysMate.name: Morphy's mate
morphysMate.desc: A bishop mates the king while a rook helps to confine it.
spot: The rook cuts off the file, and the bishop checks along the long diagonal.
morphysMate.hint: Bishop check on the long diagonal, rook cutting off the file.

operaMate.name: Opera mate
operaMate.desc: A rook checks on the back rank, defended by a bishop. Named after Morphy's Opera Game.
spot: The bishop covers the rook's mating square from a distance.
operaMate.hint: A rook on the back rank, protected by a bishop.

swallowstailMate.name: Swallow's tail mate
swallowstailMate.desc: A defended queen mates face to face, and the king's own pieces block both diagonal retreats, like a V.
spot: The queen stands directly in front of the king, supported.
The king's own rooks or pawns form the swallow's tail.
swallowstailMate.hint: A supported queen directly in front of the king.

triangleMate.name: Triangle mate
triangleMate.desc: Queen and rook, one square from the king on the same rank or file, form a triangle it can't escape.
spot: The rook protects the queen and the two together seal the box.
triangleMate.hint: Queen and rook form a triangle around the king.

vukovicMate.name: Vuković mate
vukovicMate.desc: Rook and knight combine. The supported rook mates, and the knight covers the king's escape squares.
spot: Usually on the edge, with a pawn or king supporting the rook.
vukovicMate.hint: Rook mates on the edge while the knight takes the escape squares.

cornerMate.name: Corner mate
cornerMate.desc: A rook or queen and a knight trap the king in the corner.
spot: The heavy piece seals the edge file, and the knight delivers or covers the mate.
cornerMate.hint: Confine the king to the corner, then the knight finishes it.

balestraMate.name: Balestra mate
balestraMate.desc: A bishop mates from a distance while the queen blocks the remaining escape squares.
spot: The queen stands a knight's jump from the king, covering its flight squares.
balestraMate.hint: The bishop checks from afar, and the queen covers the rest.

blindSwineMate.name: Blind swine mate
blindSwineMate.desc: Two rooks on the seventh rank mate the king in a 2×2 corner.
spot: Doubled rooks on the seventh ('pigs') sweep the rank, and the king can't leave the corner.
blindSwineMate.hint: Your two rooks on the seventh rank can work together.

castling.name: Castling
castling.desc: Castling is the winning move: king to safety, rook into play.
spot: Castling can win a tempo, unpin a piece or bring a rook to an open file with a threat.
castling.hint: Don't forget the king and rook can move together.

enPassant.name: En passant
enPassant.desc: A tactic using en passant: capture a pawn that just moved two squares past yours.
spot: It is only possible on the very next move.
En passant can open a line or capture with check.
enPassant.hint: Did the last pawn move just jump past one of yours?

promotion.name: Promotion
promotion.desc: Promote a pawn to a queen, or to whichever piece wins.
spot: Clear or deflect the blocker on the queening square.
Promoting with check or with a fork is common.
promotion.hint: Get the pawn through. What stands on, or guards, the queening square?

underPromotion.name: Underpromotion
underPromotion.desc: Promote to a knight, bishop or rook, because a queen would be wrong here.
spot: A knight promotion can fork or give check where a queen can't.
Promoting to a rook or bishop avoids stalemate.
underPromotion.hint: A queen isn't the best choice here. Which piece is?

equality.name: Equality
equality.desc: You're worse. Find the way back to a draw or a balanced position.
spot: Perpetual check, stalemate tricks and fortress ideas save half-points.
Trade into a drawn endgame when you can.
equality.hint: You can't win this, but you can save it. Look for perpetual check or a forced trade.

advantage.name: Advantage
advantage.desc: Seize your chance for a decisive advantage, about two to six pawns.
spot: The gain is real but modest: win material cleanly, without counterplay.
advantage.hint: There's a clean way to win material.

crushing.name: Crushing
crushing.desc: Punish your opponent's blunder for a crushing advantage of six pawns or more.
spot: Something big is hanging, or a combination wins major material.
crushing.hint: The opponent just blundered. What did they leave en prise?

oneMove.name: One-move puzzle
spot: Short doesn't mean easy. Check every capture and check.

short.name: Short puzzle
spot: The first move forces a reply, and the second cashes in.
short.hint: Force a reply, then cash in.

long.name: Long puzzle
spot: Calculate the forcing line to the end before you move.
long.hint: Calculate the whole forcing line before moving.

veryLong.name: Very long puzzle
veryLong.desc: Four moves or more to win.
spot: Find the target first, then plan the route.
Every move should be forcing.

master.name: Master games
master.desc: Puzzles from games played by titled players.
spot: Masters rarely blunder outright, so the tactics are often subtler.
master.hint: Look deeper than the obvious capture.

masterVsMaster.name: Master vs master
masterVsMaster.desc: Puzzles from games between two titled players.
spot: Expect well-defended positions where precision is everything.
masterVsMaster.hint: The obvious move is defended against. Find the precise one.

superGM.name: Super GM games
superGM.desc: Puzzles from games played by the best players in the world.
spot: Some of the rarest positions in the database: see what the world's best missed.
superGM.hint: Even super-GMs miss these. Take your time.

knightFork.name: Knight fork
knightFork.desc: The knight jumps in and hits two targets at once. It's the hardest fork to see coming.
spot: Check every square your knight can reach, and look two jumps ahead for a forking square.
Targets a knight's move apart from each other are classic knight-fork geometry.
knightFork.hint: Find a square from which your knight attacks two pieces.

pawnFork.name: Pawn fork
pawnFork.desc: A humble pawn attacks two pieces diagonally at once.
spot: Two enemy pieces on one rank, two files apart, in front of a pawn that can advance between them.
pawnFork.hint: A pawn push can hit two pieces at once.

queenFork.name: Queen fork
queenFork.desc: The queen's long reach creates double attacks across the board.
spot: Look for a check that also hits a loose piece.
Undefended pieces on the rim are frequent targets.
queenFork.hint: Find a queen move that attacks two things, ideally with check.

bishopFork.name: Bishop fork
bishopFork.desc: A bishop attacks two pieces along its diagonals.
spot: Two loose pieces on one colour complex, with a diagonal through both.
bishopFork.hint: Your bishop can hit two pieces on one diagonal move.

rookFork.name: Rook fork
rookFork.desc: A rook attacks two pieces along a rank and a file.
spot: Loose pieces on the seventh rank are the usual victims.
rookFork.hint: Your rook can attack two pieces at once along a rank and a file.

royalFork.name: Royal fork
royalFork.desc: King and queen forked at once, the most crushing double attack in chess.
spot: Check plus an attack on the queen: the king must move and the queen falls.
King and queen a knight's jump apart is the alarm bell.
royalFork.hint: Attack the king and queen with a single move.

queenSacrifice.name: Queen sacrifice
queenSacrifice.desc: Give up the queen for mate or to win back more.
spot: The most brilliant moves are often the ones that look impossible.
If the queen is taken, what checks do you have?

exchangeSacrifice.name: Exchange sacrifice
exchangeSacrifice.desc: Give a rook for a bishop or knight to break the position open.
spot: Usually it destroys the pawn cover or removes a key defending minor piece.
exchangeSacrifice.hint: Your rook is worth less than the piece it can remove.

opposition.name: Opposition
opposition.desc: The key move puts the kings face to face, one or three squares apart, with your opponent to move.
spot: Kings on the same file or rank with an odd number of squares between them: the side NOT to move holds the opposition.
The defending king has to give way, and yours walks in.
opposition.hint: Put your king opposite theirs, and make them move.

pawnBreakthrough.name: Pawn breakthrough
pawnBreakthrough.desc: Sacrifice a pawn to break the enemy pawn chain and promote.
spot: Three pawns against three on neighbouring files: the middle pawn often goes first.
Count it: does the new passer queen before their king catches it?
pawnBreakthrough.hint: Push a pawn into theirs. The sacrifice creates a passed pawn.

rookPawnVsRook.name: Rook + pawn vs rook
rookPawnVsRook.desc: The most common endgame in chess: Lucena, Philidor and everything in between.
spot: Attacking: build a bridge (Lucena) to shelter the king from checks.
Defending: hold the third rank (Philidor), then check from behind.
rookPawnVsRook.hint: Think Lucena (build a bridge) or Philidor (third-rank defence).

oppositeBishops.name: Opposite-coloured bishops
oppositeBishops.desc: Each side has one bishop, on different colours. Usually drawish, except when it isn't.
spot: The attacker needs two passed pawns far apart.
The defender blockades on their bishop's colour.
oppositeBishops.hint: Which squares can the enemy bishop never control?

bishopVsKnight.name: Bishop vs knight
bishopVsKnight.desc: Minor-piece endgames: the long-range bishop against the hopping knight.
spot: Pawns on both wings favour the bishop, and locked pawns favour the knight.
Knights struggle to stop rook pawns.
bishopVsKnight.hint: Use your piece's strength: range for the bishop, forks for the knight.

rookVsMinor.name: Rook vs minor piece
rookVsMinor.desc: Endgames where a rook faces a bishop or knight, the exchange up or down.
spot: The rook side wins by creating a passer or trapping the minor piece.
The minor side looks for a fortress or a fork.
rookVsMinor.hint: Use the rook's power on open lines, or the minor piece's tricks.

queenVsRook.name: Queen vs rook
queenVsRook.desc: A queen battles a rook, and forks and skewers decide it.
spot: Separate the rook from its king, then fork them.
Watch for stalemate tricks from the rook side.
queenVsRook.hint: Look for a check that forks king and rook.
